Ferenc David
fe'rents dah'veed
n. (Ferenc David, c. 1520–1579, Transylvanian preacher who denied the Trinity and founded the Hungarian antitrinitarian church)
David, a Hungarian surname from the Hebrew personal name Dawid, beloved; Ferenc, the Hungarian form of Francis, from Latin Franciscus, a Frank.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ferenc David was born at Kolozsvar of a Saxon father, studied at Wittenberg, and rose through the Transylvanian church by stages that each left a confession behind him. He was Lutheran superintendent, then Reformed superintendent, and then, from about 1565, the leader of the party which denied that the Son and the Spirit are God. In this he was pushed and organised by Giorgio Biandrata, the Italian physician who was the prince's doctor and the ablest antitrinitarian politician in Europe. David preached the new doctrine in Kolozsvar, carried the city with him, disputed against Peter Melius and the Reformed at Nagyvarad in 1569, and secured the standing of his church under the toleration voted by the Diet of Torda. He then went further than his own party would follow: he taught that Christ is not to be invoked or worshipped at all, since he is only a man. Biandrata, alarmed, brought Faustus Socinus from Poland to argue him down; David would not yield, was tried by the Diet in 1579 for innovation, and died in prison at Deva the same year. The dictionary enters him as the Hungarian Reformation's most serious wound, inflicted from inside by a man who had three times subscribed a confession of the deity of Christ.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines an antitrinitarian as one who denies the Trinity; apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed; and to blaspheme as to speak impiously of God or sacred things.

expand to see more

ANTITRINITARIAN, n. One who denies the Trinity, or the existence of three persons in the Godhead.

APOSTASY, n. [Gr. a defection.] An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.

BLASPHEME, v.t. [Gr. to speak evil.] To speak of the Supreme Being in terms of impious irreverence; to revile or speak reproachfully of God.

WORSHIP, n. Chiefly and eminently, the act of paying divine honors to the Supreme Being; religious reverence and homage.

INNOVATION, n. Change made by the introduction of something new; a novelty introduced into an established order.

Gal 1:8 — "But though we, or an angel from heaven, preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you, let him be accursed."

Modern Corruption

Transylvanian superintendent who passed from Lutheran to Reformed to antitrinitarian, taught that Christ is not to be worshipped, and died in prison in 1579.

expand to see more

This entry is itself the naming of a corruption, and the dictionary names it without hedging. The denial of the eternal deity of the Son is not a variant Christianity, an alternative reading or a point on which serious men may differ. It is the error the apostle calls by its name: “He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son” (1Jo 2:22). Thomas's confession, “My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28), was received by Christ rather than corrected, and the Father addresses the Son as God in Hebrews 1:8. David's final position—that Christ is not to be invoked—only drew out what the earlier position already contained, which is why Biandrata and Socinus, who had taught him the premise, were so anxious to disown the conclusion.

The line of this error runs forward, and should be traced rather than forgotten: Transylvanian antitrinitarianism and Polish Socinianism into English and New England Unitarianism, and from there into the liberal Protestantism which keeps the word God, keeps the word Christ, and means by the second a man uniquely filled with the first. The dictionary holds the Chalcedonian definition and the Nicene faith, and reads David's career as a warning that a confession three times subscribed is no security at all where the Scriptures are read for a system instead of heard as the voice of God.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek theos (G2316), God; Greek antichristos (G500), one in the place of or against Christ.

expand to see more

Greek kurios (G2962) — lord, master, the LORD; “My Lord and my God”, John 20:28.

Greek theos (G2316) — God; “Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever”, Hebrews 1:8.

Greek thronos (G2362) — a throne, a seat of royal power; Hebrews 1:8.

Greek antichristos (G500) — against Christ; “He is antichrist, that denieth the Father and the Son”, 1 John 2:22.

Greek anathema (G331) — a thing devoted to destruction, accursed; “let him be accursed”, Galatians 1:8.

Usage

"“And Thomas answered and said unto him, My Lord and my God” (Joh 20:28) — the confession his last position made impossible."

"“But unto the Son he saith, Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever” (Heb 1:8) — the Father's own address to the Son."

"“preach any other gospel unto you than that which we have preached unto you” (Gal 1:8) — tried for innovation in 1579 and dead in prison at Deva."
